To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(1) certain cell lines of immune, intestinal and mast cell types were able to accumulate and transmit scrapie infection to neural cells, (2) the ability to transmit scrapie infection was not dependent on the presence of PrPc, (3) the accumulation of PrPSc in these cell lines was transient and was not dependent on PrPc and (4) the accumulation of the PrPSc in the immune and intestinal cell lines was associated with the expression of the CD11a
immune, mast and intestinal cells are able to accumulate and transfer PrPSc to N2a neuroblastoma cells after prolonged exposure to PrPSc.
immune, intestinal and some neural cell lines accumulate PrPSc and are able to transfer it to neural cells.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the mechanisms of PrPSc transfer to neural cells in vitro and the role of non-neural cell types in the spread of PrP infection in vivo.
the mechanisms and processes of PrPSc uptake, intracellular traffic and intercellular transmission of infection to neural cells and the role of non-neuronal cell types in this process.
understanding the mechanism of PrPSc accumulation in cell lines and its effect on transfer of PrP to neural cells.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
PrPSc can be taken up, accumulated and transmitted to neural cells in vitro, and that the cell types that may have a role are the immune, intestinal, fibroblast and neural cells.
PrPSc can be transferred to neural cells from a variety of cell types.
PrPSc is able to be taken up and accumulated in a variety of cell types, including those not considered as the primary target for PrPSc infection in vivo.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

the immune, intestinal, neural and fibroblast cells can accumulate PrPSc for prolonged periods of time, and that the accumulation is not necessarily associated with the ability of these cells to transfer infection to other cells.
PrPSc accumulation is a complex process that involves many cell types, and the mechanisms of uptake, intracellular spread and transfer to neural cells remain unclear.
the cell type that is able to accumulate PrPSc is not necessarily able to transmit PrPSc infection.
The main takeaway from our work is that
prolonged cell culture of PrPSc-exposed cells can alter the cell response to PrPSc.
prolonged exposure to prion infectivity is required for the accumulation of infectivity in certain cell types and for the transfer of infection to other susceptible cells.
prolonged exposure of cell lines to scrapie PrPsc leads to the alteration of cell responses and the ability to transmit infection to neural cells.
